name: Zapotec civilisation
info: The Zapotec civilisation flourished in the Valley of Oaxaca in Mesoamerica from about 700 BC to AD 1521, with Monte Albán, one of the first major cities of Mesoamerica, as the centre of its state.

facts.homeland: The Central Valleys of Oaxaca in southern Mexico (Etla, Ocotlán and Mitla), about 200 km south of Mexico City; key sites Monte Albán, San José Mogote, Mitla, Lambityeco, Dainzú, Yagul, El Palmillo, Zaachila and Guiengola on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec
facts.period: Rosario phase (700–500 BC); Monte Alban 1 (late phase 400–100 BC); Monte Alban 2 (c. 100 BC – AD 200), the peak of expansion; Monte Albán the largest city of the southern Mexican highlands until about AD 700; Aztec conquest of the area in 1458; Spanish rule from 1521
facts.known: Monte Albán and its monumental buildings, ball courts and tombs; one of the first writing systems of Mesoamerica; a calendar; building J, the "Conquest Slab"; finely worked gold jewellery; the ruins of Mitla; canal irrigation
facts.sources: Excavations at Monte Albán, begun by Alfonso Caso in the 1930s; the work of Joyce Marcus and Kent V. Flannery; colonial-era sources on the gods, compiled by Michael Lind; legends written down after the Spanish conquest; finds by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH)

t: Monte Albán was founded on a mountain in the no-man's-land between three rival valley societies, and its early pottery suggests settlers came from San José Mogote.
The Zapotec developed a logosyllabic writing system thought to be one of the first in Mesoamerica; it remains undeciphered.
The Zapotec called themselves by a variant of Be'ena'a, the Cloud People, from their elite's belief that they descended from beings who lived among the clouds.
dyk: Building J at Monte Albán, shaped like an arrowhead, carries more than 40 carved stones that archaeologists read as the provinces the Zapotec controlled; upside-down heads on them are believed to stand for rulers killed in conquest.
ev: In the Rosario phase three rival societies divide the valleys of Oaxaca, and at its end San José Mogote loses most of its population
The state formed at Monte Albán begins to expand beyond the valley
Zapotec expansion peaks in the Monte Alban 2 phase, by conquest and by colonisation
Monte Albán ceases to be the largest city in the southern Mexican highlands
The last battle between the Aztecs and the Zapotec is fought at Guiengola under the Aztec ruler Ahuizotl
Francisco de Orozco arrives in the Valley of Oaxaca, and the Zapotec soon submit to the rule of Hernán Cortés

sections.origins:
Zapotec civilisation arose in the Y-shaped Central Valleys of Oaxaca, where the valleys of Etla, Ocotlán and Mitla meet at about 4,500 feet above sea level; the region is considered one of the cradles of maize. Archaeological evidence shows the culture originated at least 2,500 years ago. In the Rosario phase (700–500 BC) the valleys were divided among three societies of different size, separated by a no-man's-land of about 80 square kilometres. Burned temples and sacrificed war captives suggest that they competed against each other. At the end of the phase the largest settlement, San José Mogote, lost most of its population.

In the same period a large new settlement, later called Monte Albán, grew on a mountain in the no-man's-land overlooking the three valleys. Its early pottery resembles that of San José Mogote, which suggests its people came from there. Walls built during Monte Alban 2 suggest the city answered a military threat, and Joyce Marcus and Kent V. Flannery compare its founding to Greek synoikism, the gathering of scattered people into one city. The Zapotec languages belong to the Oto-Manguean family.
sections.society:
The Zapotec were a sedentary people living in villages and towns, in houses of stone and mortar. Between Monte Alban phases 1 and 2 the population of the Valley of Oaxaca grew considerably, and with it came greater social differentiation, more centralised political power and more ceremonial activity. In those phases the valley seems to have been split among several independent states with regional centres; by Monte Alban 3 the population and urban growth of Monte Albán itself had swelled.

Farming depended on water. The Atoyac River watered a narrow strip of land when it flooded, and elsewhere the Zapotec used canal irrigation, bringing water from small streams even to Monte Albán, 400 metres above the valley floor; archaeologists found a small dam and canal on the mountain's south-eastern flank. Because the valley alone could not feed the fast-growing population of Monte Alban 1, crops were also grown on the less fertile foothills. There was a dry season from November until May, but along the rivers two harvests a year were possible. In war the Zapotec used cotton armour.
sections.beliefs:
Zapotec religion, like most Mesoamerican religions, was polytheistic, and its gods were mostly associated with fertility and agriculture. Known deities include Cocijo, the rain god; Coquihani, the god of light; and Pitao Cozobi, the god of maize. "Pitao" is simply the word for god. From colonial-era sources Michael Lind has listed others, among them Cozichacozee, god of war, and Leraa Queche, god of medicine. Male and female deities are told apart by costume, breechcloths for men and skirts for women. There is some evidence that gods of other peoples were worshipped too, such as the Feathered Serpent of Teotihuacan and the Nahuatl god Xipe Totec. Local rulers also appear to have been deified, and it is believed that the Zapotec practised human sacrifice in some rituals.

Legends of their origin, written down only after the Spanish conquest, say their ancestors were born from rocks, emerged from caves or descended from big cats such as jaguars. The governing elite believed it descended from supernatural beings who lived among the clouds and would return to them at death. A dedication cache in Mound III at Cuilapan, dated to AD 700, held jade beads, obsidian blades, shells, a pearl and small bird bones.
sections.arts:
Monte Albán has monumental buildings, ball courts, tombs and grave goods, including finely worked gold jewellery. On its main plaza stands building J, shaped like an arrowhead, with more than 40 carved stones bearing hieroglyphic writing and heads in elaborate headdresses. Alfonso Caso, who excavated there in the 1930s, read the glyphs as the provinces controlled by the Zapotec. The well-known ruins of Mitla are also attributed to the Zapotec.

The Zapotec developed a calendar and a logosyllabic writing system, read in columns from top to bottom. It is thought to be one of the first writing systems of Mesoamerica and a predecessor of the Maya, Mixtec and Aztec scripts; some signs can be recognised as calendar information, but the script remains undeciphered and went out of use in the late Classic period. The earliest known example is a Danzante stone, Monument 3 from San José Mogote, showing what appears to be a dead captive with two glyphs, possibly his name; it was first dated to 500–600 BC, but the date is doubted. A tomb about 1,400 years old found in January 2026 has an owl-head frieze and polychrome murals of a procession carrying bags of copal.
sections.exchange:
During late Monte Alban 1 and Monte Alban 2 the Zapotec rulers took control of provinces outside the Valley of Oaxaca, and by 200 their influence reached from Quiotepec in the north to Ocelotepec and Chiltepec in the south. In many regions local pottery styles were suddenly replaced by Zapotec ones. Marcus and Flannery see both colonisation and conquest in this expansion. Relations with central Mexico were long: Teotihuacan had a Zapotec neighbourhood, and Monte Albán a Teotihuacan-style guest house. Later, Zapotec and Mixtec artisans in Tenochtitlan made jewellery for Aztec rulers, including Moctezuma II.

In the 1450s Aztec forces invaded the Valley of Oaxaca and conquered the area in 1458; in 1486 they built a fort on the hill of Huaxyácac to enforce tribute. The last battle between Aztecs and Zapotec was fought at Guiengola between 1497 and 1502. When news came that the Spaniards had defeated the Aztecs, King Cosijoeza told his people not to confront them and sent a delegation to seek an alliance. Francisco de Orozco arrived in 1521; the Zapotec and Mixtecs soon submitted, though Antequera resisted until the end of that year.
sections.legacy:
After 1526 the Zapotec lands became part of the Marquessate of the Valley of Oaxaca in the Viceroyalty of New Spain, under Hernán Cortés. Dominican friars settled in Antequera from 1528, and after the Bishopric of Oaxaca was founded in 1535 Catholic priests came in growing numbers. Settlers brought horses, cattle, goats, sheep, chickens and mules, never before seen in Oaxaca, and over the centuries native people and Spanish settlers intermarried.

Conquest brought catastrophe through disease. Smallpox, measles, typhoid, influenza, cocoliztli and other epidemics struck Oaxaca again and again: some nineteen major epidemics came before the first century of Spanish rule was over, and the native population of Oaxaca is estimated to have fallen from 1.5 million in 1520 to 150,000 in 1650 before it recovered. The Zapotec peoples of today are the descendants of the civilisation. Their languages, of which there are 7 distinct ones and over 100 dialects, are tone languages spoken in the Sierra Norte, the Central Valleys, the Southern Sierra, the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and along the Pacific coast, and through migration also in Mexico City and Los Angeles.

summary: The Zapotec civilisation of the Valley of Oaxaca built Monte Albán, one of the first major cities of Mesoamerica, and from it a state that conquered and colonised much of what is now Oaxaca. Its people developed one of the earliest Mesoamerican scripts, were conquered by the Aztecs in 1458 and submitted to the Spaniards in 1521; the Zapotec peoples of today are their descendants.
references: Lind, Michael, Ancient Zapotec Religion (University Press of Colorado, 2015)
Whitecotton, Joseph W., The Zapotecs: princes, priests, and peasants (The University of Oklahoma Press, 1984)
